blocks.text: License Plate Readers in Haverhill

Privacy matters to everyone, because you don't know who is collecting your data or who is looking at it. Blind trust in a system, and hoping it will do the right thing, has historically led to a lot of problems. It is better to have rules on the books, so it is clear what is and is not allowed no matter who is in charge. Third-party companies should not be making money off our data, especially when we have no say in how it is collected or what it is used for. Selling data is not the only way to make money from it: data used to train AI is valuable, and a contract can allow it without counting it as selling (see [The Vendor Controls the Software](#vendor-software)). Nationwide mass surveillance is wrong, and we should not take part in it, no matter which company is doing it.

This is not only about Flock. Haverhill has canceled its Flock contract, but the way that contract came about, without public notice or rules on use, could happen again (see [Added Without Oversight or Notice](#added-without-notice)). Other vendors and third parties can collect the same kind of data, so the same problems apply to whatever comes next.

This page has three goals. The first is to lay out the facts about license plate readers and other surveillance in Haverhill, with a source for each one. The second is to explain the concerns and the questions the city has not yet answered. The third is to compare the proposed rules, so residents can form their own opinion and take part before the city decides on an ordinance.
What ALPR Is and How It Works

"Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) System: A system consisting of cameras, software, databases, and related equipment designed to capture, read, compare, and store digital images and associated data from vehicle license plates."

For a plain-language history of how plate readers went from a stolen-car tool to networked tracking, see DeFlockILM's explainer ([ALPR, Explained, opens in a new tab](https://deflockilm.org/alpr-explained/), October 5, 2026), written by a citizen privacy group in North Carolina.
Why the City Wants It

"The Haverhill Police Department utilizes Flock Safety technology as an investigative tool to assist officers and detectives in solving crimes, locating vehicles associated with investigations, developing investigative leads, and protecting the community."
Other Surveillance

License plate readers are not the only surveillance technology in use in Haverhill. Some of it was chosen by the city itself, such as the Ring partnership and the cameras at Haverhill's schools. Some is available to every police department in Massachusetts through a state contract, and I could not find records showing whether or how often Haverhill uses it.

PredPol (now Geolitica), predictive policing. Haverhill. Subscription began January 6, 2014 ([PredPol renewal agreement, opens in a new tab](https://cdn.muckrock.com/foia_files/2018/11/19/HAVERHILL_PredPol_SaaS_Agreement_2016.12.08_-_renewal_contract.pdf), page 1).
Ring Neighbors Portal. Haverhill. The Police Department announced it was joining on April 17, 2019 ([Ring_4of6.pdf](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Ring_4of6.pdf#page=1), page 1).

CrimeTracer (formerly Coplink X), by SoundThinking, the company that makes ShotSpotter. Statewide. Available to police across Massachusetts through a state contract announced December 6, 2022 ([SoundThinking, opens in a new tab](https://www.soundthinking.com/press-releases/shotspotter-selected-by-commonwealth-of-massachusetts-for-statewide-deployment-of-coplink-x/)). The company says every police department in the state can use it with no opt-in required. Departments that also share their own records with it sign an agreement with the State Police and choose what to share. I found no record of whether Haverhill has signed one or how often it uses the system ([Cambridge Day, August 19, 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.cambridgeday.com/2025/08/19/crimetracer-shares-cambridge-and-somerville-police-data-statewide-and-with-ice-until-2023/)).

City surveillance cameras. Haverhill. The Police Department lists "city surveillance cameras" among the evidence it uses alongside Flock ([packet](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=33), page 33), and its case list mentions "city camera footage" ([packet](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=44), page 44).

Cameras at Haverhill schools. Haverhill. Haverhill Public Schools pays Convergint Technologies for security systems at its schools. A March 2023 proposal replaced the exterior cameras at Haverhill High School, covering the main entrance, bus lanes, and loading dock, for $14,036.09, with cameras that include "analytics with deep learning" ([proposal](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Haverhill_High_School_Exterior_Camera_Replacement_Proposal_PM05548713P_3-30-23.pdf#page=2), pages 2 to 4). Invoices also show a door card reader repair at the high school in 2023 ([invoice](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Invoice_W1627800_1.pdf)) and a three-year security service contract at Dr. Paul Nettle Middle School ([invoice](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Invc_IN00142325_-_Dr._Paul_Nettle_School.pdf), 2024). These are a selection of the records released; the full set is [on MuckRock, opens in a new tab](https://www.muckrock.com/foi/haverhill-265/public-records-request-convergint-technologies-163191/#files).

A note on ShotSpotter. ShotSpotter, also made by SoundThinking, uses microphones placed around a city to listen for gunshots. I found no record of it being used in Haverhill. Where it has been used, it has had serious problems. In Chicago, from January 2020 to May 2021, police recorded an outcome for 41,830 ShotSpotter alerts, and only 4,556 of them (9.1%) found evidence of a gun-related crime ([Chicago Office of Inspector General, August 24, 2021, page 4, opens in a new tab](https://igchicago.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Chicago-Police-Departments-Use-of-ShotSpotter-Technology.pdf#page=4)). Critics also said the sensors were placed mostly in Black and Latino neighborhoods, and Chicago let its ShotSpotter contract expire in 2024 ([NPR, October 20, 2024, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2024/10/20/nx-s1-5131546/researchers-are-skeptical-of-this-gunfire-detection-system-chicago-no-longer-uses-it)). Haverhill should not consider adding it, and the ordinance should prohibit its use.
Current Policies
Police Department Policy 41.3.9

This is the Police Department's own policy, approved by the Chief of Police ([page 1](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=46)). It is not a law passed by the City Council, and the department can amend it ([page 9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=54)). It lists the uses allowed ([page 3](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=48)), keeps data that is not evidence for 30 days ([page 8](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=53)), and requires audits inside the department at least every three months ([page 7](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=52)).
Massachusetts Law

Commonwealth v. McCarthy (2020). The state's highest court held that four cameras on two bridges were not a search, but warned that enough cameras in enough places would be ([Commonwealth v. McCarthy, opens in a new tab](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-jud-crt-mas-bar/2060202.html)).

M.G.L. c. 147, § 64 (in effect since September 4, 2026). Limits police from using state or local resources for, or taking part in, federal civil immigration enforcement except in specified circumstances, and limits sharing nonpublic information with federal immigration authorities ([special counsel's memo](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=5), PDF page 5).
Common Justifications
Reasons the city and the Police Department have given for license plate readers, in their own words, with what to know about each.

A note on where the numbers come from. Much of what the city was given about Flock came from Flock. The packet linked on this page is the one sent out before the Public Safety Committee meeting of November 12, 2026, with private material removed; I could not find a public record of it to link to instead. The department's handout relies on "Flock's own current policy" ([packet page 33](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=33)), and the packet included a Flock marketing guide for councils (packet pages 24 to 29, not reproduced here because Flock lists it as private and not for sharing). That guide tells councils "LPR is not a 'search' under the Fourth Amendment" (packet page 28), but a federal judge has since ruled that a warrantless Flock search was one ([United States v. Kyle, opens in a new tab](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/73367327/united-states-v-kyle/)). It says federal agencies are excluded from Flock's nationwide network (packet page 27), but Illinois' Secretary of State found that Flock had let U.S. Customs and Border Protection access cameras on Illinois roads, against state law ([NBC Chicago, August 25, 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/company-violated-illinois-law-by-sharing-license-plate-data-with-customs-and-border-protection-giannoulias/3814914/)). It also offers Flock's own "Outcomes" tool to produce success numbers "come time for renewal" (packet page 29).

Any company selling a product has a reason to make it look as accurate and useful as possible. That is true of Flock and of every surveillance vendor that might replace it. Numbers that come from the vendor should be treated with skepticism unless independent sources back them up.
Solving Crimes

What was said: "Flock technology has become an important investigative tool for the Police Department, providing timely vehicle identification, location information, and investigative leads that help officers identify involved parties, corroborate evidence, and move cases toward resolution." ([Police Department case list](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=43), packet page 43)

What to know: Solving crimes does not cancel the right to privacy. Police may search only in ways the law allows. The Fourth Amendment says: "The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized" ([U.S. Constitution, Fourth Amendment, opens in a new tab](https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/bill-of-rights-transcript)). Courts have not settled whether searching a license plate database is a search that needs a warrant ([Congressional Research Service, July 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF13068.html)). In October 2026, a federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a deputy's search of a month of one car's location history in Flock's database, without a warrant, violated the Fourth Amendment, and called the system "a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance" ([United States v. Kyle, opens in a new tab](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/73367327/united-states-v-kyle/), N.D. Okla.; [CBS12, October 3, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://cbs12.com/news/florida/federal-judge-rules-warrantless-license-plate-reader-search-violated-fourth-amendment-flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-database-melisa-susan-kyle-oklahoma-vehicle-data-judge-sara-hill)). In Massachusetts, the Supreme Judicial Court has said that enough cameras in enough places would be a search ([Commonwealth v. McCarthy, opens in a new tab](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-jud-crt-mas-bar/2060202.html), 2020).

How much plate readers help is also not well measured. The Congressional Research Service found no public data on how often they are used or how they contribute to cases ([Congressional Research Service, R48160](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/R48160.3.pdf#page=2), page 2). The department's case list is a selection it chose, and it does not say how many searches led nowhere.

Flock's CEO has said "Over a million cases were solved last year." When CBS News asked how that was counted, a Flock spokesperson said the technology "supported approximately 1 million investigations and incidents", including "investigative leads, cross-jurisdictional assistance, searches conducted during active investigations, and other Flock deployments" ([CBS News, September 30, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/flocks-ceo-claims-its-tech-solved-1-million-crimes-data-shows-otherwise/)). Being used in 1 million cases is not the same as solving 1 million cases, and the two should not be confused. A search that turns up nothing still counts as being "used".

The research that does exist is mixed. The best way to deal with crime is to prevent it in the first place, but the studies found little sign that plate readers do that either. A review by the National Policing Institute found:

The same review notes that studies of plate readers used in investigations are "more encouraging and less conclusive". Either way, the numbers vendors share come from their networks nationwide, so it is not clear how much plate readers actually help in Haverhill. The department saying it feels the system helps is not enough to justify it. Haverhill-specific results, including the searches that led nowhere, should be public before any system is approved.
No Expectation of Privacy on Public Roads

What was said: Flock "captures images of vehicles and license plates that pass designated cameras in areas where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy." ([Police Department Flock handout](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=32), packet page 32)

What to know: One photo of a car on a public road is generally not a search. A record of where a car goes over days or weeks is different. Under the "mosaic" idea, each location on its own shows little, but enough of them together show where someone lives, works, worships, sees a doctor, and spends the night.

The Supreme Court used this reasoning in 2018, in Carpenter v. United States. Police had collected 127 days of a man's phone location records from his phone company without a warrant. The Court said that "127 days [of cell-site data] provides an all-encompassing record of the [cell phone] holder's whereabouts", and ruled that police need a warrant for those records, even though the phone company, not the man, held them ([Congressional Research Service, July 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF13068.html)). In other words, information about where you go can still be private when a company holds it, if there is enough of it.

Courts compare plate readers to phone tracking because both record where a person goes, automatically, without the person doing anything, and both are held by someone else. A car does not go everywhere a phone does, and some courts have found plate data less revealing for that reason ([Congressional Research Service, July 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF13068.html)). Massachusetts' highest court still applied the same reasoning to plate readers in [Commonwealth v. McCarthy, opens in a new tab](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-jud-crt-mas-bar/2060202.html): enough cameras in enough places would be a search.

This matters to everyone, not only people suspected of a crime. A network that records every car that passes builds this kind of record about all of us, and tracking people in this much detail without a warrant is concerning no matter who is doing it.
Facial Recognition

What was said: "Flock does NOT use facial recognition." "Flock does NOT tell officers who a person is." ([Police Department Flock handout](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=33), packet page 33)

What to know: A plate reader does not need a face to track a person. A plate is registered to a person, and Flock records vehicle details as well as the plate ([packet page 32](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=32)). The same statement also means a plate read cannot show who was driving, which is why it should never be the only evidence placing someone somewhere (see [Additions I Would Suggest](#additions)).

The limit is in the software, not the hardware. A plate reader is a camera, and what it looks for is decided by the vendor's software. When reporters at Wired and 404 Media examined the software from a stolen Flock camera, they found it already detects people who enter the frame and records where they appear, and that the camera receives remote updates. They found no evidence of facial recognition ([Straight Arrow News, September 16, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://san.com/cc/hackers-stole-a-flock-camera-heres-what-they-found-inside/)). Flock also already sells a search for people by description, such as "man in blue shirt and cowboy hat", on its video cameras, and says it does not work on its plate readers ([Flock Safety, FreeForm Search, opens in a new tab](https://www.flocksafety.com/products/flock-freeform)). Because these are software choices, a vendor update could extend a plate reader toward searching for people, or toward facial recognition, without any new cameras being installed (see [The Vendor Controls the Software](#vendor-software)). Flock's own patent describes searching camera footage for matching faces ([U.S. Patent 11,416,545, opens in a new tab](https://patents.google.com/patent/US11416545B1/en)).
No Nationwide Data Sharing

What was said: "The Haverhill Police Department does not participate in unrestricted nationwide ALPR data sharing networks." ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=47), page 2)

What to know: The word "unrestricted" matters. The same policy allows sharing with "specifically authorized agencies and users approved by the Department" ([page 7](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=52)), and the department can change the policy itself ([page 9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=54)). Elsewhere, federal agencies have searched local plate data in sanctuary states, potentially for immigration enforcement ([NPR, November 7, 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2025/11/07/nx-s1-5587724/some-sanctuary-states-discover-feds-mining-local-license-plate-data)).

The five-year Flock order form the Police Chief signed in 2024 includes "Nationwide Network (LP Lookup Only)", which "Allows agencies to look up license plates on all cameras opted in to the nationwide Flock network" ([Flock contract, page 70](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=70)). The Police Department told the City Council on August 11, 2026 that Haverhill was not opted in ([Haverhill Community TV recording, opens in a new tab](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-august-11-2026)). The records give no way to confirm that either way, and no limits on sharing were discussed with residents before the cameras went up. That is why written limits in the ordinance matter. The city draft would require a City Council vote before joining any regional or national sharing network ([§ XXX-11](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=16), packet pages 16 to 17), and the ACLU model bill would limit sharing further (see the [comparison below](#comparison)).
Concerns
False Positives

The current police policy itself says: "Officers shall recognize that ALPR systems may generate false alerts or inaccurate reads" ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=50), page 5). How often that happens is higher than many people assume. In a randomized controlled trial run by the Vallejo, California Police Department, 35% of all alerts from readers mounted on police cars were misreads, and 37% from fixed readers ([International Association of Chiefs of Police, March 2018, opens in a new tab](https://www.theiacp.org/sites/default/files/2018-08/March%202018%20RIB.pdf)). That is roughly one wrong alert in every three.

A figure of around 90% accuracy is sometimes quoted, but the Congressional Research Service notes it is one observer's estimate rather than a formal study, and that innocent people can come under investigation when their plate matches a wrong read ([Congressional Research Service, R48160](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/R48160.3.pdf#page=11), page 11). When a read is wrong, police may stop the wrong car, sometimes at gunpoint. In February 2026 in Sherwood, Arkansas, a Flock camera misread one letter of a family's plate as a stolen car's, and officers held the couple at gunpoint and handcuffed them while their six-week-old baby was in the back seat ([KATV, opens in a new tab](https://katv.com/news/local/sherwood-stop-sparked-after-flock-camera-misread-plate-by-one-letter-as-stolen-katv-news-share-inform-public-community-safety)). More examples are under [Additions I Would Suggest](#additions).
Potential for Abuse

Plate data shows where people go: doctors, places of worship, protests, and homes. The judge in United States v. Kyle pointed to visits to medical providers, lawyers, and fertility clinics as examples of what a month of plate data can reveal ([CBS12, October 3, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://cbs12.com/news/florida/federal-judge-rules-warrantless-license-plate-reader-search-violated-fourth-amendment-flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-database-melisa-susan-kyle-oklahoma-vehicle-data-judge-sara-hill)). The current rules depend on the department checking itself, through internal audits (see [Enforcement and Verification](#enforcement)). Elsewhere, federal agencies have searched local plate data in sanctuary states, potentially for immigration enforcement ([NPR, November 7, 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2025/11/07/nx-s1-5587724/some-sanctuary-states-discover-feds-mining-local-license-plate-data)).

Officers have also used Flock to stalk and harass people. By July 2026 there were at least two dozen cases of officers resigning or being arrested for using Flock to track romantic interests ([CNN, July 26, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/26/us/flock-cameras-surveillance-abuse)). Some examples:

A Kentucky officer was arrested after allegedly tracking an ex-girlfriend through Flock more than 2,000 times ([CNN, August 26, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/26/us/flock-kentucky-police-officer-arrest)).

Five Indianapolis officers were charged with misusing Flock, mainly to search for ex-partners and people they knew. One was charged with stalking after allegedly searching a woman's plate more than 170 times and leaving a note on her car ([ABC News, September 24, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://abcnews.com/US/5-indianapolis-police-officers-charged-misusing-license-plate/story?id=136696856); [WFYI, September 24, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.wfyi.org/wfyi-news/2026-09-24/five-indianapolis-police-officers-charged-for-misusing-flock-cameras)).

A Mooresville, North Carolina officer was arrested after allegedly using Flock 31 times to track her boyfriend's ex-wife, listing most of the searches as traffic violations ([ABC News, August 6, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://abcnews.com/US/officer-allegedly-flock-license-plate-cameras-track-boyfriends/story?id=135418955)).

Many of these cases were caught by audits, which shows audits matter ([CNN, August 26, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/26/us/flock-kentucky-police-officer-arrest); [ABC News, August 6, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://abcnews.com/US/officer-allegedly-flock-license-plate-cameras-track-boyfriends/story?id=135418955)). The Mooresville case also shows that the reason an officer types in for a search can be false, so an audit that only checks that a reason was given is not enough.
Overreach

Haverhill had 19 Flock cameras at the city's entry and exit points ([Newslink, opens in a new tab](https://newslinklive.com/2026/08/13/haverhill-moves-to-regulate-use-of-flock-cameras-amid-surveillance-concerns/); [WHAV, opens in a new tab](https://whav.net/2026/08/11/haverhill-council-debates-security-vs-surveillance-cameras/)). Massachusetts' highest court has said that enough cameras in enough places would be a search ([Commonwealth v. McCarthy, opens in a new tab](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-jud-crt-mas-bar/2060202.html)). Other cities, including Cambridge, have canceled their Flock contracts over these concerns ([NPR, February 17, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2026/02/17/nx-s1-5612825/flock-contracts-canceled-immigration-survillance-concerns)).

Haverhill has now canceled its Flock contract ([City of Haverhill, November 5, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.haverhillma.gov/news/posts/city-of-haverhill-canceling-flock-safety-contract)), but that does not fix the underlying problem. The cameras were added, renewed, and given a five-year term out of public view, and residents learned about them years later (see [Added Without Oversight or Notice](#added-without-notice)). It should not have taken a public outcry for this to come to light. Without written rules requiring public notice and a vote first, the next system, from any vendor, could be added the same way.
Enforcement and Verification

Under the current policy, audits are done inside the Police Department, at least every three months, by the ALPR Administrator (the Captain of the Criminal Investigations Division), and the audit records are kept by the department ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=49), pages 4 and 7). The policy does not require any public report, so the only way for a resident to check that it is being followed is a public records request ([page 9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=54)). The policy also lists what the Flock contract "shall require" of the company ([page 8](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=53)), but names no way for the city or the public to check that the company does it.

The draft ordinance would add a yearly report to the Mayor and City Council ([§ XXX-14](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=18)) and terms vendors must agree to ([§ XXX-12](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=17)). A vendor that breaks those terms would be dealt with through its contract. The draft also states that it gives residents no right to sue if the rules are broken ([§ XXX-18(E) and (F)](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=21)). That is a concern for a system residents cannot opt out of: anyone who drives past a camera is recorded, whether or not they agree to it.

Vendors do not always follow what a city decides. After Cambridge deactivated its Flock cameras, Flock installed two more without the city's knowledge, from a work order that should have been canceled, and Cambridge ended the contract ([City of Cambridge, December 10, 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.cambridgema.gov/news/2025/12/statementontheflocksafetyalprcontracttermination)).
Added Without Oversight or Notice
The Flock cameras were in place for years before residents were asked about them. The Flock contract's own attachments show the steps:

January 2022: the Police Chief signed a Flock order form for 8 cameras, for 24 months, renewing automatically unless canceled ([page 20](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=20), [page 22](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=22), [page 33](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=33)). The department's current plate reader policy took effect in December 2022 ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=46), page 1).

January 2024: the Police Chief signed a new order form for 11 cameras with a 60-month (five-year) term, $137,500 in total ([page 66](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=66), [page 68](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=68)).

April 2025: the City Council's first vote on Flock, more than three years after the first order. It only allowed the Mayor to sign a contract longer than three years. The order gives no reason for the longer term and sets no rules on use ([page 72](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=72)).

June 2025: the city signed a $110,000 contract running through December 31, 2029, which can be "extended, in writing, at the sole discretion of the City" ([page 3](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=3)).

August 2026: the first public discussion. The City Council agenda for August 11 lists only the Mayor's request for the Acting Deputy Police Chief to "discuss Flock cameras and software utilized by the Haverhill Police Department for license plate monitoring" (item 5.1, [agenda, opens in a new tab](https://media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/haverhillma-003-us/media/oqypskkh/full-agenda-8112026.pdf), page 1). The department's handout is marked by hand as handed out at that meeting, but it is not in the published agenda ([packet page 32](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=32); [WHAV, opens in a new tab](https://whav.net/2026/08/11/haverhill-council-debates-security-vs-surveillance-cameras/)).
I have not found any public notice to residents explaining why the cameras were added, why a five-year term was needed, or where the cameras were placed.

This is not the first time. When the Police Department joined Ring's Neighbors app in 2019, the announcement was a press release, and the department's email that afternoon asked only: "Please post this to facebook." ([Ring_4of6.pdf](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Ring_4of6.pdf#page=1), pages 1 to 3). Another notice may have gone out, but I did not find one in these records. A Facebook post is not the same as informing the City Council or raising it at a public meeting. Opting a city into surveillance should take more than a Facebook post.

The release itself appears to have been written by Ring's public relations team. A draft dated "April X, 2019" has the same text ([page 4](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Ring_4of6.pdf#page=4)), Ring's public relations coordinator is listed as a media contact, and it ends with Ring's own claim that "one Los Angeles neighborhood saw a 55 percent decrease in home break-ins", with no independent source ([page 2](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Ring_4of6.pdf#page=2)).
The Vendor Controls the Software

This section uses Flock as the example because its contract with Haverhill is public. The concern is not limited to Flock. Any third-party surveillance company is likely to have similar terms, keeping control of its own software and treating how it works as proprietary, so the same questions apply to any vendor the city might use next.

What a plate reader can search for is decided by the company's software, not by the city. Flock's "Vehicle Fingerprint" already searches for more than plates: "type, make, color, state registration, missing/covered plates, bumper stickers, decals, roof racks, and bike racks" ([Flock contract, page 43](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=43)).
The contract leaves the software in Flock's hands:

"Flock may make any upgrades to system or platform that it deems necessary or useful", including for "the competitive strength of, or market for, Flock's products" ([page 44](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=44)).

Flock's "Proprietary Information" includes "non-public information regarding features, functionality and performance of the Services" ([page 47](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=47)), and the city may not examine how the software works ([page 48](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=48)).
Flock may use anonymized data from the cameras for "the training of machine learning algorithms" ([page 47](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=47)).

The Police Department's handout says Flock does not use facial recognition ([packet page 33](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=33)), but that describes the product as it is today. Software that searches for bumper stickers could be changed to search for people, or to recognize faces, if the company chose to. Flock's plate reader software already detects people in the frame and receives remote updates ([Straight Arrow News, opens in a new tab](https://san.com/cc/hackers-stole-a-flock-camera-heres-what-they-found-inside/)), and Flock already offers people search on its video cameras ([Flock Safety, opens in a new tab](https://www.flocksafety.com/products/flock-freeform)). The current police policy limits how plate reader data is used and shared, but it does not limit which features the vendor provides or bar searching for people ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=46), pages 1 to 9). Because the vendor's software is proprietary, neither the city nor residents can check what it does.

Flock's patents show where its software could go. U.S. Patent 11,416,545, granted to Flock Group Inc in 2022 with its CEO and a co-founder as inventors, describes one system that searches video from many unrelated cameras, including home security systems and store cameras. It describes searching that footage for "a person with matching face recognition data points", and sending an alert when a person seen on camera "is statistically similar to the teenage daughter of a subscriber" ([U.S. Patent 11,416,545, opens in a new tab](https://patents.google.com/patent/US11416545B1/en); see also [DeFlockILM, September 17, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://deflockilm.org/flock-tracking-patent/)). A patent describes what a company could build, not what it has built, and Flock says its plate readers do not use facial recognition. But it shows the company has already designed for it, and that the only thing between a plate reader and a people tracker is software the city does not control.

Selling data is not the only issue. The 2024 agreement says Flock "does not own and shall not sell Customer Data" ([page 46](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=46)), but it also gives Flock a "worldwide, perpetual, royalty-free right to use and distribute" anonymized data "to improve and enhance the Services and for other development, diagnostic and corrective purposes, and other Flock offerings" ([page 47](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=47)). The 2022 agreement gave Flock a "perpetual" license, lasting "during and after the term", to disclose the department's data and footage to law enforcement ([page 31](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=31)).

The police policy says the agreement with Flock "shall require" that the vendor "not independently sell, mine, monetize, or commercially distribute Department ALPR data" ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=53), page 8). The contract itself allows Flock to use the data to train AI, to build other products, and to distribute it, and nothing in the contract or the policy limits who Flock shares it with for those purposes. The contract does not say how the data is anonymized, and because it is proprietary, no one outside Flock can check. Once data has been used to train a system or shared with others, it cannot be taken back, even after the contract ends.
Questions for the City

These questions apply to any license plate reader system, not only Flock. The city has said it is canceling the Flock contract, and that the Public Safety Subcommittee will discuss guardrails "for any future ALPRs" ([City of Haverhill, November 5, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.haverhillma.gov/news/posts/city-of-haverhill-canceling-flock-safety-contract)). Flock is on the agenda of the City Council's Public Health, Safety & Works Committee meeting of November 12, 2026. The concerns on this page come from what license plate readers do, whichever company provides them.

Did the city consider [Commonwealth v. McCarthy, opens in a new tab](https://privacysos.org/blog/mass-high-court-license-plate-reader-surveillance-can-trigger-constitutional-protections/)? In 2020, Massachusetts' highest court held that four cameras on two bridges were not a search, but warned: "With enough cameras in enough locations, the historic location data from an ALPR system in Massachusetts would invade a reasonable expectation of privacy." Haverhill had 19 Flock cameras at the city's entry and exit points. Was that question asked before they were installed?

When the City Council voted on April 8, 2025 to allow a Flock contract longer than three years ([Document 23-F](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=72)), was it told how the cameras would be used, how long the data would be kept, or who it would be shared with?

At its September 3, 2026 meeting, before voting on a license, the License Commission asked the applicant about installing cameras and whether they planned to work with the police ([Haverhill Community TV recording, opens in a new tab](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-license-commission-meeting-september-3-2026), from 13:25). Is agreeing to share footage a condition of getting a license, and does the city have any written limits on how that footage is requested or used?
If Flock is replaced, will any new license plate reader system, from any company, have to meet the ordinance and be approved in public before it is installed?
Comparing the City's Draft Ordinance and the ACLU Model Bill

Two proposed sets of rules for license plate readers. The city's draft ordinance was written by the city's special counsel with the Police Department, and sent to the Mayor and City Council in September 2026 ([memo](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=3), [draft](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=8)). The ACLU's model bill is a template any city can adopt ([ACLU, opens in a new tab](https://www.aclu.org/documents/local-automatic-license-plate-reader-privacy-model-bill), November 2026, [copy](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf)). Each summary below gives the section and page it comes from.

The topics below are not a complete list of what the two bills say. They are a selection I chose of the differences I think matter most: how much a system can collect, keep, and share, who can check it, and how the rules are enforced. The "My recommendation" box under each topic is my opinion of which is better and why, favoring the option that collects less or gives the public more oversight. Please read both full texts, linked above, and form your own opinion.
What counts as a license plate reader
City draft ordinance

Any system of cameras, software, databases, or related technology that reads a plate or other information about a vehicle, whether fixed, mobile, vehicle-mounted, or portable, including its software, databases, analytical tools, and alerts.
[§ XXX-2(A), packet page 9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=9)
ACLU model bill
Any system or software that turns images of plates into computer-readable data. Cameras that only switch on for a specific violation, like speeding or running a red light, are not included.
[Section 1(A), page 1](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=1)
My recommendation: Both combined

Start with the ACLU wording, "Any system or software that turns images of plates into computer-readable data", because it says plainly that software counts even when it is used on its own. The city draft lists software as part of a system, but the ACLU wording leaves no doubt. Then add the city's "whether fixed, mobile, or portable, along with its software and databases", so databases of the images are covered too. Keeping the city's "other vehicle information" would also cover systems that identify cars by make, color, or features.
What it can be used for
City draft ordinance

Purposes listed in a police use policy the City Council approves, including investigating crimes, stolen vehicles, missing persons, hit-and-runs, and other law-enforcement or public-safety purposes named in that policy.
[§ XXX-7(B), packet pages 13 to 14](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=13)
ACLU model bill

Only checking plates against specific lists (stolen, unregistered or uninsured, uninspected, an outstanding felony warrant, a missing person, or a felony), plus parking enforcement, access to secured areas, and toll collection.
[Section 2(B), pages 1 to 2](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=1)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill
It is a closed list. The city draft allows any purpose named in a police use policy, which can be widened later without changing the ordinance.
What is not allowed
City draft ordinance

Personal, political, retaliatory, discriminatory, or commercial use; harassment; tracking someone for lawful protected activity; building a pattern of someone's movements unless reasonably necessary for an authorized purpose; generalized surveillance without an authorized purpose; and selling the data or using it for advertising.
[§ XXX-7(C), packet page 14](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=14)
ACLU model bill

Any use not on the allowed list. For registration, insurance, and inspection checks, enforcement aimed at a group based on race, ethnicity, or income beyond its share of the population is also banned.
[Section 2(A) and (C), pages 1 to 2](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=1)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill, plus the city's list
The ACLU bill bans every use that is not on its allowed list. Keeping the city's named bans as well makes the most common misuses explicit.
Who approves the system
City draft ordinance

The City Council must approve buying, borrowing, accepting as a donation or trial, or expanding a system, any new data-sharing agreement, and the police use policy. A public impact report is posted 14 days before the vote, and the use policy is posted on the city's website.
[§ XXX-4 to XXX-6, packet pages 10 to 13](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=10)
ACLU model bill
No section on this. The bill sets the rules directly instead.
My recommendation: City draft, with more public oversight

The City Council did vote on Flock in April 2025, but only to allow a contract longer than three years. That vote set no rules on how the cameras could be used and required no public report (Flock contract, page 72). The public discussion came in August 2026, more than four years after the first Flock order (Flock contract, pages 20 to 22). The draft's Council vote and 14-day public notice are a start. A public hearing before any approval, a public list of camera locations, and a yearly report posted where residents can read it would give residents a say before a system is in use, not after.
Software updates and minor changes
City draft ordinance
Changes the Police Chief decides are minor, including software or firmware updates, need no City Council approval. They are logged and summarized in the yearly report.
[§ XXX-4(C), packet page 11](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=11)
ACLU model bill
No section on this. Any system that does not fully follow the bill cannot be used at all.
[Section 2(D), page 2](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=2)
My recommendation: Stronger than both

Software decides what a plate reader can search for, so a software update that adds a new kind of search is not minor, even if the Police Chief decides it is. Every software or firmware update should be listed in a written public record, and any update that adds a feature or a new kind of search should need City Council approval.
How long data is kept
City draft ordinance
No fixed limit. Data is kept "no longer than reasonably necessary", with the actual period set in the police use policy.
[§ XXX-10, packet page 16](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=16)
ACLU model bill
Deleted after 48 hours, unless it is needed as evidence of a listed offense, for tolls, at another agency's sworn request for an active case, or under a warrant.
[Section 3(A), pages 2 to 3](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=2)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill
48 hours is a fixed, short limit. The city draft sets no number, and the current police policy keeps data for 30 days (Policy 41.3.9, page 8).
Sharing with other agencies
City draft ordinance

No automatic, unrestricted, or bulk access. Data can be shared when the law, a warrant, court order, or subpoena, or the police use policy allows it. Joining a regional or national sharing network needs City Council approval.
[§ XXX-11, packet pages 16 to 17](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=16)
ACLU model bill
Only specific data (one camera or area, up to 48 hours) to a Massachusetts agency or one within 25 miles that agrees not to pass it on, or to anyone with a probable cause warrant.
[Section 5 and Section 1(E), pages 1 and 4](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=4)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill
It allows only specific data, to nearby or in-state agencies that agree not to pass it on, or with a warrant. The city draft allows sharing under a police use policy.
Vendors and third parties
City draft ordinance

Vendor contracts must keep the city in control of its data and ban unauthorized sale, disclosure, or secondary use of it, and any use for advertising or unrelated commercial purposes. They must also require security, audit logs, notice of breaches, and return or destruction of the data when the contract ends. A vendor cannot make a material change to how data is collected, kept, used, or shared without City Council approval.
[§ XXX-12, packet pages 17 to 18](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=17)
ACLU model bill
A vendor running the system for the city may not share the city's data with anyone without the city's express permission, and only in ways the bill allows.
[Section 5(A)(2)(a), page 4](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=4)
My recommendation: Both combined

Both bar vendors from sharing the city's data on their own: the city draft by banning unauthorized disclosure and secondary use, and the ACLU bill by requiring the city's express permission for any sharing. Neither names AI training. "Secondary use" could cover it, but the ordinance should say plainly that city data cannot be used to train AI or to build other products, because the Flock contract allowed both (Flock contract, pages 31 and 47).
Private plate reader cameras, like businesses or homes
City draft ordinance
Not covered, unless the system or its data is given to the city, run for the city, or used under an agreement with the city.
[§ XXX-3(D), packet page 10](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=10)
ACLU model bill

Police need a warrant to demand access to a private plate reader camera or its data. They can only accept it if it is offered freely, for no payment, about a crime on that property or against its customers or employees. Private plate readers in places open to the public need a sign within 10 feet of each camera.
[Section 4, pages 3 to 4](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=3)

Sharing footage with police: at its September 3, 2026 meeting, before voting on a license, the License Commission asked the applicant about installing cameras and whether they planned to work with the police (Haverhill Community TV recording, from 13:25). Neither bill limits police asking for ordinary security camera footage. The ACLU model's limits apply only to private plate readers, and the city draft would apply only to data once the city has it.
My recommendation: ACLU model bill

It requires a warrant before police can demand data from a private plate reader. The city draft does not cover private plate readers at all. Ordinary security and doorbell cameras are not covered by either bill, which is a gap worth closing.
Immigration enforcement
City draft ordinance
Use for federal civil immigration enforcement is banned, except as Massachusetts law (M.G.L. c. 147, § 64) allows.
[§ XXX-7(C)(6) and (E), XXX-8(E), XXX-9(E), packet pages 14 to 16](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=14)
ACLU model bill
No separate section. The limits on use and sharing apply to every agency.
My recommendation: City draft
It is the only one with explicit protections tied to Massachusetts law (M.G.L. c. 147, § 64).
Data security
City draft ordinance
"Reasonable" safeguards, individual logins, and required training.
[§ XXX-13, packet page 18](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=18)
ACLU model bill
End-to-end encryption while data is stored and sent.
[Section 3(C), page 3](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=3)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill
End-to-end encryption is a specific standard that can be checked. "Reasonable" safeguards cannot.
Audits and public reporting
City draft ordinance
Audited at least once a year, and a yearly report to the Mayor and City Council by March 1, including the number and general locations of cameras, searches, sharing, and costs.
[§ XXX-14, packet pages 18 to 19](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=18)
ACLU model bill
No section on this.
My recommendation: City draft

The yearly report on audits and usage should be in writing, not only presented verbally, and should be a public record posted where residents can read it, not only sent to the Mayor and City Council. The audits should also be done independently of the Police Department.
Emergencies
City draft ordinance

The Police Chief can use a system without Council approval when there is an imminent threat of death, serious injury, or other substantial harm. Use must stop when the emergency ends, and the Chief must give a written report to the Mayor and Council within 90 days.
[§ XXX-15, packet pages 19 to 20](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=19)
ACLU model bill
No section on this.
My recommendation: City draft, with stronger limits

If emergency use is allowed, it needs a written report to the Mayor and City Council, and that report should be available to everyone as a public record. The ordinance should also limit how often emergency use can happen. The city draft requires the use to stop when the emergency ends and a written report within 90 days, but the Police Chief decides when an emergency exists, the report is not public, and there is no limit on how often it can happen. Its ban on using emergencies to monitor protest or religious activity should stay.
Systems already in use
City draft ordinance
An inventory within 180 days, and existing systems brought into line within 180 days unless the Council extends it.
[§ XXX-16, packet page 20](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=20)
ACLU model bill
Existing contracts that do not follow the bill must be amended or ended.
[Section 2(D), page 2](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=2)
My recommendation: Both combined

Keep the city draft's inventory and widen it. Within 180 days, the Police Chief would have to list every plate reader system in use, where it is, the vendor, the agreements, any data sharing, and any regional, statewide, or national databases the department can search (§ XXX-16(B), packet page 20). The inventory should cover every surveillance technology and third-party system the ordinance would affect, not only plate readers, so it would also answer questions this page could not, such as whether Haverhill uses CrimeTracer. It should be in writing and a public record. Then add the ACLU rule: contracts that do not follow the rules must be changed or ended, rather than allowing 180 days that the Council can extend.
Evidence collected against the rules
City draft ordinance
The ordinance creates no rule about evidence in court.
[§ XXX-17(F), packet page 21](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=21)
ACLU model bill
Data collected or shared in violation cannot be used as evidence, except to help a defendant.
[Section 6, pages 4 to 5](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=4)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill
Evidence collected in violation cannot be used, which gives the rules consequences in court.
If the rules are broken
City draft ordinance
Discipline for city staff and contract remedies for vendors. The draft states it gives residents no right to sue.
[§ XXX-18(D) to (F), packet page 21](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=21)
ACLU model bill
A person harmed can sue for actual damages or $1,000, plus lawyer's fees.
[Section 7, page 5](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=5)
My recommendation: ACLU model bill

Residents can sue, so enforcement does not depend only on the city disciplining its own staff or its vendors. That matters for a system residents cannot opt out of: anyone who drives past a camera is recorded.
Additions I Would Suggest
Neither bill includes these. They are my suggestions.

A person must approve every enforcement action. No fine, ticket, warrant, arrest, or other action should be taken based only on an automated system or AI. The city draft says an alert alone is not probable cause, but asks for a person to check it only "when reasonably practicable" ([§ XXX-8(F) to (H)](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=15)), and the current police policy says "whenever practicable" ([Policy 41.3.9](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=50), page 5). A plate is not a person. A camera records where a car was, not who was driving it. Cars are borrowed, shared, and sold, and plates can be misread. The Police Department's own handout says Flock "does NOT tell officers who a person is" ([packet](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=33), page 33). License plate data should never be the only evidence used to place someone somewhere. Misread plates. In San Francisco in 2009, a license plate reader misread Denise Green's plate, 5SOW350, as 5SOW750, a stolen car. Officers held her at gunpoint and handcuffed her without checking the plate. A federal appeals court ruled that "an unconfirmed hit on the ALPR does not, alone, form the reasonable suspicion necessary to support an investigatory detention" ([Green v. City and County of San Francisco, Ninth Circuit, 2014, opens in a new tab](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2014/05/12/11-17892.pdf)). Plate mix-ups. In Aurora, Colorado, police held a Black family, including children, at gunpoint because their plate number matched a stolen motorcycle from another state. The city paid a $1.9 million settlement ([CNN, February 5, 2024, opens in a new tab](https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/05/us/colorado-aurora-settlement-stolen-vehicle-mixup)). Wrongful arrests. Detroit police arrested Robert Williams in front of his family after facial recognition software matched him to the wrong person ([NPR, June 24, 2020, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2020/06/24/882683463/the-computer-got-it-wrong-how-facial-recognition-led-to-a-false-arrest-in-michig)). A 2024 settlement now requires Detroit police to have independent evidence before an arrest ([ACLU, opens in a new tab](https://www.aclu.org/cases/williams-v-city-of-detroit-face-recognition-false-arrest)). Wrong tickets. AI cameras on New York City buses read plates and issued about 800 tickets in error because of a programming error, even though a person was supposed to review each one ([NPR, December 31, 2024, opens in a new tab](https://www.npr.org/2024/12/31/nx-s1-5213674/transit-systems-ai-cameras-bus-lanes)).

Software updates need public review. The city draft lets the Police Chief treat software and firmware updates as minor changes that need no City Council approval ([§ XXX-4(C)](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=11)). Because software decides what a plate reader can search for (see [The Vendor Controls the Software](#vendor-software)), every update should be listed in a written public record, and any update that adds a feature or a new kind of search should need City Council approval.

No AI training or other products from city data. The city draft bans "secondary use" of city data by vendors ([§ XXX-12](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/ProposedOrdinanceFromHaverhillLawyers.pdf#page=17)), and the ACLU bill bars vendors from sharing it without the city's express permission ([Section 5(A)(2)(a)](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/Local-Automatic-License-Plate-Reader-Guardrails-Model-Bill-1126.pdf#page=4)). Neither names AI training. The ordinance should say plainly that city data, including anonymized data, cannot be used to train AI or to build other products, because the Flock contract allowed both ([Flock contract, page 31](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=31); [page 47](ref:PublicSafetyLPR/FlockContractwithHaverhill.pdf#page=47)).

Cover all tracking technology, including aerial surveillance. The ordinance should apply to any technology that can track people or vehicles, including aerial surveillance from drones or aircraft, facial recognition, and gunshot detection. Police drone programs are spreading quickly, and drones can see into yards and through windows ([EFF, July 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/07/hundreds-drone-first-responder-programs-could-soon-be-launched-across-country); [ACLU, 2023, opens in a new tab](https://assets.aclu.org/live/uploads/2023/07/embargo-drones-as-first-responder-programs-final-electronic.pdf)). Some drones now carry license plate readers themselves ([EFF, September 2025, opens in a new tab](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/09/drone-sky-could-be-tracking-your-car)), which a rule written only for fixed cameras could miss. A federal appeals court ruled that police aerial surveillance covering much of Baltimore for 12 hours a day needed a warrant, and other courts have warned that cameras combined with "facial recognition, automated tracking or artificial intelligence" could cross the same line ([Congressional Research Service, May 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB11429)).
No gunshot detection. The ordinance should prohibit systems like ShotSpotter (see the note under [Other Surveillance](#other-surveillance)).
Public Trust

Public trust is not only a concern for residents. It matters to the police too. The National Policing Institute calls public support "an operational concern". In a 2018 survey of 405 people, 90% did not know whether their local police used plate readers at all, and the researchers recommended that agencies weigh public perception seriously before adopting the technology, because awareness would catch up ([National Policing Institute, August 27, 2026, opens in a new tab](https://www.policinginstitute.org/infocus/alpr-backlash-what-agencies-need-to-know/)). In Haverhill, we can see where this is an issue given the contentious City Council meeting in August, and it is something we should be concerned about for the future.

Police depend on residents to report crimes, come forward as witnesses, and share information. That works best when people trust how they are being watched and why. Surveillance added without notice puts that trust at risk, even when it is meant to help.

The goal is transparency and collaboration: rules everyone can see and rely on, where residents know what is collected and who can see it, the City Council decides in public, and officers have tools the community has agreed to. That takes residents, the Council, and the Police Department working together, and the ordinance is the place to start.
